pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** Grouping Living Things (by observable features)

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y4 'Living things and their habitats'):** pupils recognise that living things can be grouped in a variety of ways.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-LS4-1 context):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS4-1]; classifying by observable characteristics underpins pattern-finding across organisms (US delays formal taxonomy, so DfE is the primary anchor).

- **Operational details:** The central idea is that grouping is a CHOICE of criterion, not a fixed truth: the same set of organisms can be grouped many valid ways (by habitat, body covering, diet, number of legs, has-a-backbone), and the SAME organism lands in different groups depending on the criterion used. Pupils must (a) group a set by at least two different criteria, (b) state the criterion they used, and (c) recognise a group can be re-cut a different way. This is the conceptual seed of classification and, later, of variation — it teaches that categories are tools we impose to make sense of diversity.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A–B (concrete moving to relational). Pupils sort concrete/pictured organisms and articulate their criterion; the relational step is realising the SAME organism regroups under a new criterion. Success = groups one set two different ways and explains why the same animal moved groups.
bestPractices: Make the CRITERION explicit every time — always ask 'what rule are you grouping by?' so pupils see the rule, not the piles, is the point.
Have pupils group the SAME set at least two different ways so they experience that groups are not fixed.
Use a criterion that visibly moves one organism between groups (a frog: 'lives in water' vs 'has no fur') to make the choice-not-truth idea concrete.
Let pupils invent their own criteria and test them for consistency — ownership of the rule deepens the concept.
Introduce the vertebrate/invertebrate and animal-group vocabulary as ready-made criteria without letting them crowd out free grouping.
keyRepresentations: Sorting mat / bins with a selectable criterion header
The same organism shown in two different groups under two criteria (highlighted moving)
Feature cards per organism (covering, legs, diet, backbone) — the attributes to group by
Carroll/Venn-style two-way sort for a single criterion pair (e.g. has wings / lays eggs)
commonMisconceptions: Believing each organism has one 'correct' group it truly belongs to, rather than grouping being a choice of criterion.
Grouping by superficial similarity (colour, size) and treating that as equivalent to biologically meaningful features.
Thinking that if an animal moves groups the animal itself has changed, rather than the criterion changing.
Assuming 'lives in water' means 'is a fish' — conflating habitat with classification group.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9, teach that grouping living things is a CHOICE of criterion, not a fixed truth: the same set of organisms can be validly grouped many ways (habitat, body covering, diet, number of legs, has-a-backbone), and the SAME organism lands in different groups depending on the rule used. The core learner work is to (a) group a set by at least two different criteria, (b) state the criterion used each time, and (c) recognise that one organism regroups when the criterion changes. This seeds classification and, later, variation. The central activity is an active re-sort; the alternatives support pre-teaching the attributes to sort by, checking placements, and defending a chosen rule in discussion.

activities.title: Multi-criteria sorting bench: group the same set two ways
feedback: If a learner treats one grouping as the 'real' one, show two valid groupings of the same set side by side using criteria they actually applied (e.g. by body covering; by diet) and ask which rule each pile follows — both are legitimate.
If a learner says the animal 'changed' when it moved piles, point back to the single organism and ask: 'What about the frog is different now? Or did only our rule change?'
If a learner sorts sensibly but cannot name the rule, ask 'What is the same about everything in this pile?' to surface the criterion already in use — scaffold, don't reteach.
If a learner sorts by colour or size, contrast that with fur/backbone and ask which features tell you more about the animals themselves.
activities.rationale: Grouping-as-choice is felt through active re-sorting of one set under successive rules; physically or on-screen dragging the same animals into new piles is intended to make the criterion, not the piles, the object of attention. A selectable criterion header and highlighting one organism as it moves between sorts make the mechanism concrete. A free-choice mode gives the learner ownership of the rule.
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 'Living things and their habitats' requires pupils to recognise that living things can be grouped in a variety of ways.
Grouping by observable characteristics is the foundational classification skill; the same organism can belong to different groups depending on the criterion chosen.
learnerActions: Take a tray of 8–12 familiar organisms (pictured or on cards) and sort them into groups under one chosen rule, e.g. body covering: fur / feathers / scales / bare skin.
State out loud or write the rule you are grouping by before you start each sort.

Now change the criterion to 'what it eats', then to 'how many legs', then to 'lives in water or not', and re-sort the SAME animals each time; watch which animals leave one pile and join a different one.

Track one organism across the sorts you actually perform, e.g. a frog: under the body-covering sort it sits in the 'bare skin' pile, but under a 'lives in or near water' habitat sort it joins the fish (many adult frogs also spend time on land, so agree the rule's wording first) — note that the frog itself did not change, only the rule did.
As an extension, try a two-way (Carroll or Venn) sort that crosses two criteria at once, e.g. 'has wings' against 'lays eggs', and notice that where one organism lands depends on both rules together.
In a 'make your own group' mode, invent your own rule, sort by it, and check that every animal in a pile really shares that feature (test your rule for consistency).
activities.intendedInsight: Groups are not fixed labels stuck to each creature; a group is a tool we impose by choosing a criterion. The same organism belongs to different groups depending on the feature we sort by.

activities.title: Feature reveal: pre-teach the attributes you can sort by
feedback: If a learner cannot find a feature to group by, prompt them to compare two animals' feature cards and spot a shared attribute.
If a learner only notices colour/size, draw attention to covering, legs, diet and backbone as the biologically meaningful attributes.
activities.rationale: An annotated set where each organism reveals its features pre-teaches the sortable attributes so the later re-sort is about choosing rules, not discovering facts. This is a reference/pre-teach step: it supplies the attributes but does not itself let the learner experience grouping as a choice.
learnerActions: Look at each organism in the set and name its features: body covering, number of legs, diet, and whether it has a backbone.
Make a feature card for each organism recording those attributes (e.g. tapping a pictured organism to reveal a card, or writing one by hand).
Before sorting, predict which feature would put two particular animals in the same group and which would split them.
activities.intendedInsight: Before you can group by a rule, you need to know each organism's features — some you can see (body covering, number of legs) and some you find out (diet, whether it has a backbone) — and these attributes are what the rules act on.

activities.title: Check and defend: place, justify, and relate groupings
feedback: If a learner sorts a bat with birds because it flies, contrast flight (shared by unrelated animals) with fur/milk, and ask which features a bat shares with a dog that a robin does not.
If a learner insists each animal has one correct box, show the bat in both 'can fly' (with robin, butterfly) and 'feeds its young milk' (with dog, whale) and point out both sorts are valid.

If a learner concludes a whale 'is a fish', clarify that grouping it with fish only reflects the 'lives in water'/shape criterion, while breathing air and feeding its young milk group it with mammals and reflect how the animals are really related.
If a learner can't say why a placement is right, ask 'What rule did you use to decide?'
activities.rationale: Placement items and a 'defend your grouping' discussion let you check whether the learner can both sort and articulate the criterion, and whether they accept one organism in two groups. These check and extend the idea; recognition/placement alone does not, by itself, surface the criterion-is-a-choice insight, so pair it with the active re-sort and justification talk.
learnerActions: Place given organisms into vertebrates/invertebrates (or another named pair), then state the criterion that pair uses.
Use a two-way (Carroll/Venn) grid for a single criterion pair, e.g. 'has wings' and 'lays eggs', and explain why a chosen animal lands in its cell.

Answer: 'Does a whale go with the fish or with the dog? What does it depend on?' and explain your reasoning — grouping a whale with fish reflects only a 'lives in water'/body-shape criterion, while grouping it with the dog reflects 'breathes air / feeds its young milk', so the answer depends on the rule you choose.
Place the SAME animal into two different correct groups under two different criteria and say why each placement is right.
Discuss: 'Is there a wrong way to group these animals, or just different ways?' and 'Which grouping tells you more about how the animals are really related — can fly or feeds milk? Why?'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to place organisms correctly AND name the criterion, and to show one organism fits two groups, demonstrates that grouping depends on the chosen feature rather than a single hidden truth; some features (feeds milk) also reflect how animals are actually related.

constraints: Make the CRITERION explicit every time — always ask 'what rule are you grouping by?' so the rule, not the piles, is the focus.
Have learners group the SAME set at least two different ways so they experience that groups are not fixed.
Choose at least one criterion that visibly moves one organism between groups (e.g. a bat: 'can fly' puts it with birds, but 'has fur' puts it with dogs) to make choice-not-truth concrete.
Let learners invent their own criteria and test them for consistency to build ownership.
Introduce vertebrate/invertebrate and animal-group vocabulary as ready-made criteria without letting them crowd out free grouping.

Guard against conflating habitat with classification (e.g. 'lives in water' means 'is a fish') and against treating superficial similarity (colour, size) as equivalent to biologically meaningful features.

The feature-reveal step is a pre-teach scaffold: it supplies attributes but does not let the learner perform the re-sort that reveals grouping as a choice. Recognition/placement items check sorting but do not require independent construction of a new criterion; pair them with the active re-sort and a spoken or written justification. None of these media is asserted as universally superior to the others.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One source claim (that grouping by observable characteristics is foundational and the same organism can belong to different groups) is marked verified:false in the source row; treat its evidential weight cautiously even though it aligns with the verified DfE standard.

The original row asserted that a 3D medium 'adds nothing' and that sorting is 'better done by hand than described'. These are unproven catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws, and are not reproduced as universal claims. Hands-on dragging, on-screen dragging and spoken justification each offer different, complementary affordances with no proven superiority established here.

The whale example is treated as a criterion-dependent case (fish by habitat/shape vs mammal by fur/milk); ensure learners are not left believing a whale is a fish — the point is that the GROUP depends on the chosen feature, while fur/milk reflects how the animals are actually related.
The frog-tracking step follows the frog across criteria the learner actually applies (body covering and habitat), keeping the activity internally coherent.
The Carroll/Venn two-way sort (e.g. has wings / lays eggs) from the original representations was restored; it had been dropped in an earlier candidate.
Activity[0] feedback was adjusted so the two side-by-side groupings reference criteria run in that activity (body covering, diet) rather than 'flight', which is only used in the bat assessment case.

probeDeeper: Group these three by ONE feature, then re-group the same three by a DIFFERENT feature.
Does a whale go with the fish or with the dog? What does it depend on?
Is there a 'wrong' way to group these animals, or just different ways?
Which grouping tells you more about how the animals are really related — 'can fly' or 'feeds milk'? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: A bat is a mammal. But which GROUP it lands in depends on the criterion you sort by: group by 'can fly' and the bat joins the robin and butterfly; group by 'has fur / feeds milk' and it joins the dog and whale. The same organism belongs to different groups depending on the feature chosen — there is no single fixed grouping.

errorPatterns.pattern: Surface-similarity sorting — 'it flies like a robin, so a bat is a bird.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast flight (shared by unrelated animals) with fur/milk; ask which features a bat shares with a dog that a robin does not.
errorPatterns.distractor: A bat is a bird, because it flies like the robin.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Assigns the bat to birds on the basis of flight alone.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Each animal has one correct group' — grouping is fixed, so you must pick the single right box.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show two valid groupings side by side (by flight, by fur); both are legitimate — the group depends on the sorting rule, not on one hidden truth.
errorPatterns.distractor: A bat can only be in one group — you have to pick the one right group for it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists the bat can only go in one group and there is a single right answer to which.

errorPatterns.pattern: Groups sensibly but cannot state the criterion — 'they just go together.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: ask 'what is the same about everything in this pile?' to surface the criterion already in use.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sorts correctly yet cannot name the feature the grouping is based on.

responseLevels.gap: Assigns one fixed group by surface features and rejects the idea of multiple groupings.
responseLevels.full: Groups by two or more criteria, names each criterion, and explains that the same organism belongs to different groups depending on the feature chosen, transferring the idea to the whale case.
responseLevels.partial: Groups by two criteria when prompted but treats one grouping as the 'real' one, or cannot state that the same organism moves between groups.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'A bat, a robin and a butterfly can all fly. But a bat, a dog and a whale all have fur or feed their babies milk. So which group does the bat belong in — and could it belong to more than one group? Explain how you decided.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks each animal has one 'true' group, or who sorts by surface resemblance ('it flies, so it's a bird'), cannot accept the bat in two different groupings. A child who understands grouping-by-criterion explains that the group changes with the feature you sort by — the whole point of this topic.
